opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we wrestled with a lot. When large language models took off, the honest answer was that the existing compiler stack wasn't designed for them. Traditional deep learning compilers, including the earlier TVM, assumed a fairly static world: you get a fixed computational graph with known shapes, optimize it end to end, and ship it. LLMs break many of those assumptions. You have dynamic sequence lengths, KV caches that grow over time, different behavior in prefill and decode, and fast-moving kernel techniques like FlashAttention and paged attention. You also want to run the same model on a server GPU, a laptop, a phone, or a web browser.

So we could patch things: add a special case for dynamic shapes, bolt on a custom attention kernel. That gets you a demo quickly. But each patch makes the system more brittle, and eventually the special cases outnumber the general machinery. At that point the compiler stops buying you anything.

On the other hand, a full rewrite has its own risks. You throw away years of hard-won engineering: code generation for many backends, the scheduling infrastructure, the community knowledge. And you might rebuild the same mistakes with a nicer coat of paint.

The way I think about it is to ask which abstractions are fundamentally wrong and which are still right. For us, what needed rethinking was the core program representation. We needed to treat dynamic shapes as first-class, and we needed to let graph-level optimizations, tensor-level programs, and hand-written or vendor libraries live together in one system instead of being separate silos. That's the idea behind what we called TVM Unity and the Relax representation. You don't force everything through one automatic path; you let engineers mix and match, call cuBLAS or a FlashAttention kernel where it makes sense, generate code where it makes sense, and still optimize the whole thing.

But a lot of the lower layers, like code generation, the target backends, and the runtime pieces, were still valuable. We kept and evolved those. So I'd describe it less as "rebuild versus patch" and more as "rebuild the foundations that encode the wrong assumptions, and reuse everything that's still sound."

There's also a meta-lesson. In machine learning systems, the workloads change every couple of years. So the real goal isn't to build the perfect compiler for LLMs; it's to build something composable enough that when the next shift comes, you can adapt without starting over. Projects like MLC LLM were partly a test of that: can a small team take a new model and get it running efficiently across many devices quickly? When that works, it tells you the abstractions are right.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts patches that can deliver a quick demo for current needs with rebuilding the foundations to support changing workloads and future shifts.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it wasn't really a clean binary choice between rebuild and patch. It was more about asking what the core abstractions should be, and then deciding how much of the old stack still fit those abstractions.

When we started TVM, the world looked very different. Models were mostly static graphs, shapes were known at compile time, and the main problem was generating fast kernels for a fixed set of operators across a lot of hardware. The whole design, the separation between the graph level and the tensor level, the autotuning machinery, all of that was optimized for that world. And it worked well for that world.

Large language models break several of those assumptions at once. You have dynamic shapes everywhere because of sequence length and batching. You have a KV cache that has to be managed across many invocations, so the compiler has to reason about state, not just a pure function. You have memory planning that matters as much as kernel speed, because you're often memory bound. And you have this constant need to pull in external pieces, whether that's a hand-written attention kernel, a quantization library, or something a vendor just released, because nobody can keep up by generating everything from scratch.

So the question we asked was: can we incrementally patch dynamic shapes into a system that assumed static shapes? We tried, and you can get a certain distance, but you end up with special cases layered on special cases. At some point the complexity of the patches exceeds the complexity of just getting the abstraction right. That's what led to Relax as a new graph-level IR, and to the unity approach where the graph level and the tensor level live in the same module and can be optimized together. That's the "rebuild" part.

But I want to be careful with the word rebuild, because a lot of the lower layers carried over. TensorIR, the scheduling and tuning infrastructure, the runtime, the codegen backends for CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, WebGPU, those were still fundamentally sound. What we did was rethink the layers where the assumptions had broken, and keep the layers that still made sense. I'd call it more of a rearchitecture than a rewrite.

There's also a philosophical shift that I think is the real trade-off. The old mental model was that the compiler should own everything and generate the best possible code. The new model is that the compiler should be a good coordinator. It should be easy to bring in a FlashAttention kernel or a vendor library and have it work alongside generated code, and the compiler should focus on the things it's genuinely good at: fusion, memory planning, handling dynamism, and portability across devices. Being willing to give up some of that control was hard, but it's what made MLC LLM possible, where the same model runs on a phone, a laptop, a browser, and a server GPU.

So if I had to summarize: patching is cheaper in the short term but you pay interest on every workaround. Rebuilding is expensive but only worth it if you've actually identified which abstractions are wrong. The discipline is in figuring out that boundary, replacing exactly what needs replacing, and keeping everything else.

r001.rationale: It contrasts cheaper short-term patching with reworking abstractions that no longer fit LLM requirements, framing the choice as immediate convenience versus preparing the compiler for newer needs.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do we need to change, and what can we reuse? Large language models introduce requirements that may not fit the assumptions of an existing compiler. If we only patch around those assumptions, eventually the system becomes difficult to improve. But rebuilding everything also means losing a lot of useful infrastructure and spending time solving problems we already know how to solve.

So I would approach this by looking at the workload end to end. Where does the existing abstraction help, and where does it get in the way? Keep the components that still work well, and be willing to redesign the boundaries that prevent you from expressing what the model needs.

The goal isn’t to preserve TVM exactly as it is, or to start over for the sake of starting over. It’s to make the system useful for the next set of workloads, while retaining the parts of the compiler technology that give us a strong foundation.

r001.rationale: The response weighs future LLM workloads against preserving useful existing infrastructure, but it does not clearly frame this as preparing for future needs versus meeting current needs in the short term.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is which assumptions have changed. With large language models, you have dynamic sequence lengths, KV cache management, and different requirements for prefill and decoding. Those things affect more than individual operators; they affect how you organize the runtime and the whole compilation flow.

If we only patch the existing stack, we may end up preserving abstractions that make those problems harder to solve. But rebuilding everything also means losing a lot of useful infrastructure and engineering experience.

So I would take a pragmatic approach: be willing to rethink the abstractions where the workload demands it, while reusing the parts that still work well. Build an end-to-end path for the new workload, understand where the real bottlenecks are, and let that guide what needs to change. The goal is not to preserve the old compiler or to create a new one for its own sake. It is to make these models run efficiently and make the system easy to evolve.

r001.rationale: The response weighs rethinking abstractions for new workloads against reusing useful existing infrastructure, but it does not clearly frame this as preparing for future needs versus meeting current short-term needs.
